## Three eras, two media

`ggthemes` has always had `theme_economist()` and `theme_economist_white()`,
built from *The Economist*'s house style as it looked around 2012. This
vignette adds two more eras, each with its own print and web variant:

| Era | Functions | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Classic (~2012) | `theme_economist()`, `theme_economist_white()` | already in the package |
| "New design" (2017) | `theme_economist_2017()` with `media = "print"` or `"web"` | *The Economist visual styleguide*, v1.2, 4 May 2017, an internal PDF (Matt McLean) that documents this redesign explicitly, including an "OLD DESIGN / NEW DESIGN" comparison that lines up with the classic theme on one side and this one on the other |
| 2024 redesign | `theme_economist_2024()` with `media = "print"` or `"web"` | no public chart styleguide covers this refresh, so these values are measured from published Economist charts: 94 print charts and about 420 web graphics from April 2024 to August 2026, including indexed PNGs and responsive `ai2html` graphics |

The "new design" print and web palettes use different hues. Print's primary
order is *dark blue, cyan, gold, teal, maroon, mauve*; web's is a nine-color
*red, blue, cyan, green, yellow, olive, purple, gold, gray*. The 2024 redesign
uses a stable six-color order in both media: *red, salmon, blue, light blue,
dark gray, light gray*. Print and web have different production values, and a
brighter red marks plain single-series charts. Red and gray sequential ramps
and a red-gray diverging ramp cover ordered data.

The 2017 guide is a specification; adoption lagged it. Sarah Leo, a visual
data journalist at the paper, wrote about the transition from the inside in
["Mistakes, we've drawn a
few"](https://medium.economist.com/mistakes-weve-drawn-a-few-8cdd8a42d368)
(*The Economist*, 27 March 2019): "Most of the 'original' charts were
published before our chart redesign. The improved charts are drawn to fit
our new specs." Those "new specs" are the 2017 redesign, seen in production
two years after the guide. The measured chart corpus agrees: the series-color
shift from `#01A2D9` to `#076FA1` dates to 2019, not 2017.

One chart type from the styleguide's own catalog isn't included below:
tables aren't a ggplot2 geom. Thermometer charts aren't a built-in geom
either, but they're just a range plot (a segment between two values with a
mark at each end), so `geom_segment()` and `geom_point()` reproduce them
exactly. They get a section of their own.

```{r setup}
library(ggthemes)
library(ggplot2)
```

## All the palettes, side by side

The chart below compares ten discrete palettes across the three eras, with
one row per `media`, `set` and `type` combination, so they can be compared
directly instead of reconstructed from separate examples further down.

```{r palette-comparison, fig.height=4.2, fig.width=7.5}
pals <- list(
  "Classic" = economist_pal()(9),
  "New, print (bar_side)" = economist_2017_pal("print", type = "bar_side")(6),
  "New, print (stacked)" = economist_2017_pal("print", type = "stacked")(6),
  "New, print (line_side)" = economist_2017_pal("print", type = "line_side")(6),
  "New, print (dot)" = economist_2017_pal("print", type = "dot")(6),
  "New, print (pie)" = economist_2017_pal("print", type = "pie")(6),
  "New, print (bright)" = economist_2017_pal("print", set = "bright")(4),
  "New, print (dark)" = economist_2017_pal("print", set = "dark")(3),
  "New, web" = economist_2017_pal("web")(9),
  "2024, print" = economist_2024_pal("print")(6),
  "2024, web" = economist_2024_pal("web")(6)
)

pal_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pals), function(nm) {
  hex <- pals[[nm]]
  data.frame(pal = nm, i = seq_along(hex), hex = hex, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
pal_df$pal <- factor(pal_df$pal, levels = rev(names(pals)))
## White text on dark tiles, black on light -- relative luminance, not just
## darkness, so a saturated mid-tone (e.g. the reds) still reads correctly.
rgb <- t(col2rgb(pal_df$hex)) / 255
luminance <- rgb %*% c(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)
pal_df$label_colour <- ifelse(luminance < 0.5, "white", "black")

ggplot(pal_df, aes(x = i, y = pal, fill = hex)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.94, height = 0.8, colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = hex, colour = label_colour), size = 2.4, vjust = 2.1, family = "mono") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

## The 2024+ palettes: examples and sources

The 2024 redesign has qualitative, sequential and diverging palette families.

| Palette | Functions | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Qualitative | `economist_2024_pal()`, `scale_*_economist_2024()` | Six recurring series colors, ordered red, salmon, blue, light blue, dark gray, light gray; separate print and web values. |
| Sequential | `economist_2024_seq_gradient_pal()`, `scale_*_gradient_economist_2024()` | Light-to-dark red and gray ramps reconstructed from maps, heatmaps and shaded bands. |
| Diverging | `economist_2024_div_gradient_pal()`, `scale_*_gradient2_economist_2024()` | Gray-to-red around the medium's ground color, for change or deviation from a meaningful midpoint. |

All three families take `media = "print"` or `"web"`.

```{r economist-2024-palettes, fig.height=2.2, fig.width=7.5}
categorical <- economist_2024_pal("web")(6)
sequential <- economist_2024_seq_gradient_pal()(
  seq(0, 1, length.out = 32)
)

palette_swatches <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    palette = "Discrete: series and highlights",
    x = (seq_along(categorical) - 0.5) / length(categorical),
    width = 1 / length(categorical),
    hex = categorical
  ),
  data.frame(
    palette = "Sequential: low to high",
    x = (seq_along(sequential) - 0.5) / length(sequential),
    width = 1 / length(sequential),
    hex = sequential
  )
)
palette_swatches$palette <- factor(
  palette_swatches$palette,
  levels = rev(unique(palette_swatches$palette))
)

ggplot(palette_swatches, aes(x = x, y = palette, fill = hex, width = width)) +
  geom_tile(height = 0.68) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(
      hjust = 1,
      colour = "#0D0D0D",
      margin = margin(r = 8)
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 5.5, 5.5, 5.5)
  )
```

Use the discrete palette when color identifies separate series:

```{r economist-2024-discrete-example, fig.height=3.2, fig.width=6.5}
series_example <- data.frame(
  year = rep(2021:2025, 3),
  value = c(31, 35, 34, 41, 45, 24, 27, 31, 30, 36, 18, 20, 19, 24, 27),
  series = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 5)
)

ggplot(series_example, aes(year, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(
    data = subset(series_example, year == 2025),
    aes(label = series),
    hjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_economist_2024() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2021:2025,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(position = "right") +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Three series use distinct 2024+ inks",
    subtitle = "Illustrative data",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_economist_2024("web")
```

Use the sequential palette when color encodes an ordered quantity:

```{r economist-2024-sequential-example, fig.height=3.2, fig.width=6.5}
surface_example <- expand.grid(x = 1:18, y = 1:8)
surface_example$exposure <- with(
  surface_example,
  16 * exp(-((x - 12)^2 / 32 + (y - 5)^2 / 7))
)

ggplot(surface_example, aes(x, y, fill = exposure)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient_economist_2024(
    name = "Exposure",
    breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15)
  ) +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Pale-to-dark red encodes increasing magnitude",
    subtitle = "Illustrative data",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_economist_2024("web") +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

## Toy data

Each dataset below is built to have the same *shape* as one of the
styleguide's own named examples, so the same story can be told in five
styles side by side. None of the numbers are real. They are illustrative,
sized and shaped like the original chart.

```{r toy-data}
## Like "Salud" (p.13): one series, one country highlighted
doctors <- data.frame(
  country = factor(
    c("Sweden", "Denmark", "Britain", "Portugal", "Luxembourg",
      "France", "Austria", "Spain", "Germany"),
    levels = c("Sweden", "Denmark", "Britain", "Portugal", "Luxembourg",
               "France", "Austria", "Spain", "Germany")
  ),
  visits = c(2.9, 4.3, 5.0, 5.4, 5.9, 6.4, 6.6, 7.3, 8.0),
  highlight = c(rep(FALSE, 7), TRUE, FALSE)
)

## Like "Defenders of democracy" (p.13): two series, grouped bars
elections <- data.frame(
  country = rep(c("Chile", "Brazil", "Mexico", "Poland", "India"), each = 2),
  income = rep(c("Middle class", "Low income"), 5),
  pct = c(78, 68, 71, 60, 66, 58, 55, 47, 51, 44)
)
elections$country <- factor(elections$country, levels = rev(unique(elections$country)))

## Like "The Fed says no to nuptials" (p.14): stacked bar, market share
carriers <- data.frame(
  carrier = factor(
    c("AT&T", "Verizon", "Sprint Nextel", "T-Mobile", "Other"),
    levels = c("Other", "T-Mobile", "Sprint Nextel", "Verizon", "AT&T")
  ),
  share = c(30.4, 31.4, 10.0, 11.1, 16.8)
)

## Like "Where Tokyo leads" (p.6/15): two lines over time
bonds <- data.frame(
  year = rep(1:15, 2),
  yield = c(
    8.1, 7.6, 6.8, 6.9, 5.4, 4.6, 4.9, 3.8, 3.2, 2.9, 2.1, 1.8, 1.6, 1.2, 0.9,
    2.0, 1.9, 1.7, 1.6, 1.4, 1.3, 1.5, 1.2, 1.1, 0.9, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1
  ),
  country = rep(c("Japan", "United States"), each = 15)
)

## Like "Foreign hoards" (p.16): stacked area, currency reserves
reserves <- data.frame(
  year = rep(2002:2011, 2),
  trn = c(
    0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.2, 1.6, 1.9, 2.3, 2.8,
    0.5, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6, 1.9, 2.1, 2.4, 2.7
  ),
  region = rep(c("China", "Other developing countries"), each = 10)
)
reserves$region <- factor(reserves$region, levels = c("Other developing countries", "China"))

## Like "Divergent" (p.18): scatter with two time periods and trend lines
metro <- data.frame(
  employment = c(
    -1, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 6.5, 7, 7.5,
    0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
  ),
  house_prices = c(
    -3, -1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18,
    -2, 0, 1, 3, 3, 5, 6, 8
  ),
  period = c(rep("Q1 1990 - Q1 2007", 16), rep("Q1 2012 - Q1 2016", 8))
)

## Like "Naan bigger" (p.20): donut chart, workforce by division
workforce <- data.frame(
  division = c("Tata Steel", "Jaguar Land Rover", "Tata Consultancy Services",
               "Others", "Taj (hotels)", "Tata Chemicals"),
  thousands = c(19.4, 19.0, 4.9, 0.6, 0.4, 0.5)
)
workforce$division <- factor(workforce$division, levels = workforce$division)

## Like "The horrible science" (p.17): a thermometer chart -- a range
## between two values per category, with a mark at each end. Not a
## built-in geom, but geom_segment() + geom_point() draws it exactly.
adjectives <- data.frame(
  field = c("Mathematics", "Economics", "Computer Science", "Business", "Biology",
            "Philosophy", "English", "Psychology", "History", "Communication"),
  one = c(48, 71, 65, 58, 52, 90, 118, 74, 61, 55),
  two = c(112, 168, 140, 121, 133, 149, 205, 143, 139, 128)
)
adjectives$field <- factor(adjectives$field, levels = rev(adjectives$field))
```

## A helper to show all six styles

The helper draws the same base plot six ways: classic print, classic
web/white, "new design" print, "new design" web, 2024 print, 2024 web. The
classic era gets two variants from the package's original pair of theme
functions: `theme_economist()` (the bluish-gray print look) and
`theme_economist_white()` (its white-panel web variant, already documented
as what *The Economist*'s Graphic Detail blog used). Both draw on the same
`economist_pal()` colors, because that palette was never split by print and
web the way `economist_2017_pal()` is. The helper is a plain function local
to the vignette, not part of the package.

`new_type` picks which of the five per-chart-type print orders in
`economist_2017_pal()` to use for the print variant of the "new design". See
the box below each section heading for which one and why.

```{r variant-helper}
show_variants <- function(p, aes_type = c("colour", "fill"),
                           new_type = c("bar_side", "stacked", "line_side", "dot", "pie")) {
  aes_type <- match.arg(aes_type)
  new_type <- match.arg(new_type)
  scale_fn <- function(theme_name, ...) {
    get(paste0("scale_", aes_type, "_economist", theme_name))(...)
  }
  variants <- list(
    "Classic (~2012) -- print" =
      p + theme_economist() + scale_fn(""),
    "Classic (~2012) -- web/white" =
      p + theme_economist_white() + scale_fn(""),
    "New design (2017) -- print" =
      p + theme_economist_2017(media = "print") + scale_fn("_new", media = "print", type = new_type),
    "New design (2017) -- web" =
      p + theme_economist_2017(media = "web") + scale_fn("_new", media = "web"),
    "2024 redesign -- print" =
      p + theme_economist_2024(media = "print") + scale_fn("_2024", media = "print"),
    "2024 redesign -- web" =
      p + theme_economist_2024(media = "web") + scale_fn("_2024", media = "web")
  )
  for (nm in names(variants)) {
    print(variants[[nm]] + labs(caption = nm))
  }
}
```

## Bar / column, side by side, one series with highlight

```{r bar-highlight, fig.height=4}
p <- ggplot(doctors, aes(x = country, y = visits, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(position = "right") +
  labs(
    title = "Salud", subtitle = "Doctors' consultations per person, selected countries",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  )

## The highlight uses each theme's own accent/first colour, keeping the
## point of the original ("one bar picked out") without hard-coding a hex.
p_classic <- p + theme_economist() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = economist_pal()(1)))
p_classic_white <- p + theme_economist_white() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = economist_pal()(1)))
p_new_print <- p + theme_economist_2017(media = "print") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = economist_2017_pal("print", type = "bar_side")(1)))
p_new_web <- p + theme_economist_2017(media = "web") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = economist_2017_pal("web")(1)))
p_2024_print <- p + theme_economist_2024(media = "print") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = economist_2024_pal("print")(1)))
p_2024_web <- p + theme_economist_2024(media = "web") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = economist_2024_pal("web")(1)))

p_classic + labs(caption = "Classic (~2012) -- print")
p_classic_white + labs(caption = "Classic (~2012) -- web/white")
p_new_print + labs(caption = "New design (2017) -- print")
p_new_web + labs(caption = "New design (2017) -- web")
p_2024_print + labs(caption = "2024 redesign -- print")
p_2024_web + labs(caption = "2024 redesign -- web")
```

## Bar / column, side by side, two series

```{r bar-grouped, fig.height=4}
p <- ggplot(elections, aes(x = country, y = pct, fill = income)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(position = "right") +
  labs(
    title = "Defenders of democracy",
    subtitle = "Say having a choice of at least two parties is very important, %",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  )
show_variants(p, aes_type = "fill", new_type = "bar_side")
```

```{r bar-stacked, fig.height=3.6}

  scale_y_continuous(position = "right") +
  labs(

```

## Line, side by side

```{r line, fig.height=4}

  scale_y_continuous(position = "right") +
```

## Line, stacked (area)

```{r area-stacked, fig.height=4}
p <- ggplot(reserves, aes(x = year, y = trn, fill = region)) +
  geom_area() +
  scale_y_continuous(position = "right") +
  labs(
    title = "Foreign hoards", subtitle = "Developing-country currency reserves, $trn",
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  )

```

## Thermometer

Thermometer charts are not a built-in ggplot2 geom, but are structurally a
range plot: a segment between two values per category, with a colored mark
at each end. This is the guide's own "dot terminals" variant (p.17) instead
of the tick-mark default. It is cleaner to reproduce, and the guide names it
as an accepted alternative "when lines are unclear".

```{r thermometer, fig.height=4.2}
adjectives_long <- data.frame(
  field = rep(adjectives$field, 2),
  which = rep(c("one", "two"), each = nrow(adjectives)),
  value = c(adjectives$one, adjectives$two)
)

p <- ggplot(adjectives, aes(y = field)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = one, xend = two, yend = field), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 3) +
  geom_point(data = adjectives_long, aes(x = value, y = field, colour = which), size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(position = "top") +
  labs(
    title = "The horrible science",
    subtitle = 'Use of a specific "adjective" per million words in student reviews',
    x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL
  )
show_variants(p, aes_type = "colour", new_type = "dot")
```

## Scatter, with trend lines

```{r scatter, fig.height=4}
p <- ggplot(metro, aes(x = employment, y = house_prices, colour = period)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(position = "right") +
  labs(
    title = "Divergent",
    subtitle = "United States, housing and employment, metro-area average annual change, %",
    x = "Employment", y = "House prices", colour = NULL
  )
show_variants(p, aes_type = "colour", new_type = "dot")
```

## Pie / doughnut

```{r pie, fig.height=4.5}
p <- ggplot(workforce, aes(x = 2, y = thousands, fill = division)) +
  geom_col(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  xlim(0.5, 2.5) +
  labs(title = "Naan bigger", subtitle = "Tata's workforce in Britain, September 2011, '000", fill = NULL) +
  theme_void()

## Pie/doughnut charts don't use axes, so only the fill palette and the
## title styling carry over -- shown here just via the discrete fill scales.
p + scale_fill_economist() + labs(caption = "Classic (~2012) -- print")
p + scale_fill_economist() + labs(caption = "Classic (~2012) -- web/white")
p + scale_fill_economist_2017(media = "print", type = "pie") + labs(caption = "New design (2017) -- print")
p + scale_fill_economist_2017(media = "web") + labs(caption = "New design (2017) -- web")
## No 2024 version: none of the 88 print or 118 web charts surveyed from
## after the redesign is a pie or doughnut.
```

## Notes

- **For the 2017 design, print and web use different colors.**
  `economist_2017_pal(media = "print")` and `economist_2017_pal(media = "web")`
  share no hex values.
- **The 2024 redesign uses the same six roles in both media, with different
  production values:** no print value occurs in the web exports, and no web
  value in the print charts. The grounds differ too (`#ECEBE0` warm gray for
  print, white for web).
- `economist_2017_pal(media = "print", set = "bright")` and `set = "dark"`
  expose the styleguide's two higher-contrast alternates. They are meant for
  "multi-category charts where high contrast is needed" (its own words), not
  everyday use, and are left out of the chart examples above to keep this
  vignette to one story per chart type.

### Does the color order depend on chart type? Checked in all three eras

- **2017 "new design" (print): yes.** Pages 13-20 of the guide each
  illustrate one chart-type family and each carries its own numbered
  "COLOUR ORDER" swatch strip. Pixel-sampling all of them found 5 distinct
  sequences over the *same* 6 hues. The hues never change, only the order,
  which is why `economist_2017_pal(media = "print")` takes a `type` argument
  (`"bar_side"`, `"stacked"`, `"line_side"`, `"dot"`, `"pie"`; see above).
  Two pairs turned out hex-identical: bar/column stacked and line stacked
  share one order, thermometer and scatter share another.
- **2017 "new design" (web): no evidence either way.** The guide shows a
  single "MAIN" swatch row for web (p.12) and never illustrates a web chart
  type with its own numbered order the way it does for print. `type` has no
  effect when `media = "web"`.
- **Classic (~2012): mixed.** `economist_pal()` predates this vignette and
  already varies by `fill` (bars and areas versus lines and points), with
  each ordering commented with the chart it was sourced from. The corpus
  (224 classic-era charts, 2012-2018) was checked against real chart-type
  families instead of just the fill/color split. Bar/column side-by-side
  has a clean, repeated answer: three grouped-bar charts with keys
  ("One stock, big effect", "What's in a letter?", "The best lack all
  conviction") all order `#01A2D9` (blue) before `#014D65` (dark blue),
  exactly matching `economist_pal(fill = TRUE)(2)`'s existing
  `c("blue", "dark blue")`. That validates the existing code and adds no
  new finding. The other four buckets don't converge the same way. Stacked
  charts are blue-family-led, but the third and later colors differ from
  chart to chart (green and gray in one, coral and maroon in another, a
  six-step ordinal ramp in a third). Line side-by-side and dot/scatter
  charts mostly label series inline instead of using a key, so there is no
  unambiguous reading order to extract. What is consistent is a role, not a
  position: red/maroon marks whichever series the story is about, and
  blue/cyan is the default. Pie/doughnut is too rare to derive an order
  from, since pies were nearly gone after 2012 (see the classic style
  guide). `economist_pal()` is unchanged here. Where the evidence is clean,
  the package already had it right, and adding a `type` argument for the
  other four would overstate how consistent real charts are.
- **2024 redesign: one order, but two reds.** No public styleguide covers
  this era, so the only check is the measured chart corpus. It shows no
  type-specific order, but it does separate two reds: a brighter orange-red
  (`#F04F38` print, `#F6423C` web) for plain single-series charts, and the
  deeper red for emphasis in charts with several series. They share a chart
  in only 3 of 94 print charts. `economist_2024_pal()` keeps one order and
  returns the single-series red when asked for one color.
